title: A fluctuation chart is a video turned into numbers: read the picture, then the trace it produced
summary: Each point on a height or width trace is one video frame reduced to one number. The sampled frames in these figures let you check that the number follows the picture; the seismograph strips show the same traces being drawn as the flame moves.

media.alt: Three-part figure titled MVI_8036 flame height and width fluctuation. Top row: six photographs of a yellow-white flame at 303, 350, 396, 443, 489 and 535 seconds, some with a kinked tip. Middle: flame height in millimetres against time, a dense black trace between about 60 and 155 mm. Bottom: flame width in millimetres, a dark red trace mostly between 10 and 14 mm with bursts up to about 20 mm near 445 s. Dashed leader lines join each photograph to its time on both traces.

source.caption: Sampled frames to measured fluctuation
source.note: How the fluctuation charts are built. Figure 06 links six sampled video frames of run MVI_8036 (t = 303 to 535 s) by leader lines to their points on the flame-height and flame-width series. Figures 13 and 19 are single frames of the scrolling 'seismograph' view for two runs: a flame image on the left, a height strip at the top right and a width strip (time running down the page) at the bottom right.
group: 13_MVI8036-seismograph-onset: Real-time seismograph, onset window (MVI_8036, about 163 to 183 s)
19_MVI8037-seismograph-developed: Real-time seismograph, developed window (MVI_8037, about 383 to 403 s)

read_the_figure.question: How do the flame's height and width change from moment to moment, and does the plotted number follow what the camera actually saw?
read_the_figure.axes: Figure 06: x is time in seconds after ignition (about 300 to 535 s), top trace y is flame height in mm (about 55 to 160), bottom trace y is flame width in mm (about 10 to 20). Seismograph figures: the top strip has time on x and height in mm on y, the bottom strip has width in mm on x and time on y, so that time runs down the page and the strip scrolls with the video.
look_at: The six photographs and their leader lines: each dashed line joins a frame to the instant on the traces that it produced. Check that tall, thin frames sit at height peaks and short ones at dips.
The height trace (black): its upper edge is the flame tip, its lower envelope the flame being short. Fast jagged wiggles are the flicker; slower drifts are the mean height changing.
The width trace (dark red): much smaller in amplitude than height and with different timing. A width burst without a height burst means the flame bulged rather than stretched.
The red dot at the right edge (or bottom edge) of each seismograph strip: it marks 'now', the frame being shown on the left.

The axis ranges of figures 13 and 19: the width axis runs about 0 to 20 mm for the onset window but 0 to about 65 mm for the developed run. The strips are not drawn on a common scale, so amplitudes cannot be compared across the two by eye.
read_the_figure.proves: If each sampled photograph agrees in size and shape with its point on the traces, the pipeline is measuring the thing it claims to measure. It does not by itself show how accurate the scale is: that needs the calibration.
if_wrong: A frame whose tip is clearly higher or lower than the trace says: the edge detector picked up glow or a detached flame piece instead of the flame body.
A trace that jumps by a large step in one frame and returns: a segmentation failure or a detached fragment, not physics.
Height and width traces with the same shape: the width is probably being taken from the same mask in a way that couples to height.
Charts with different axis ranges set side by side: a visual comparison of amplitudes is misleading.
must_check: Millimetre scale (pixel size) and how it was set; neither figure states it.
What 'height' means: tip above the burner rim, along the centreline, or along the contour. Here the figure does not say.
Frame rate and time stamps: the sampled frames are spaced by 46.4 s, which is (535 minus 303) divided by five, so that the spacing is regular.
The two traces share one time axis, and sampled frames are marked on it.
Same axis limits when two runs are compared.
as_drawn: Values read off by eye, about 5 percent.

Figure 06: sampled frames at 303, 350, 396, 443, 489 and 535 s. The height trace has a long-run centre near 105 to 115 mm with excursions from about 55 to 157 mm. The width trace sits at about 11 to 13 mm for most of the window and reaches about 20 mm near 445 s.
Figure 13: the window is about 163 to 183 s. Height wanders between about 55 and 88 mm, and width between about 10.5 and 13.5 mm.
Figure 19: the window is about 383 to 403 s for run MVI_8037. Height varies between about 80 and 160 mm, mostly 90 to 135 mm, and width between about 14 and 22 mm.

terms.meaning: One still image of the video. At a frame rate f_s the time between frames is 1/f_s.
Deciding which pixels belong to the flame. The result is a binary mask whose outline is the contour.
How many millimetres one pixel spans at the flame's distance from the camera, found from an object of known size.
The distance from the burner rim to the flame tip, here shown in mm.
The width of the mask, in mm. Whether it is the maximum width or a width at a given height must be stated.
The signal minus its slowly varying mean. Its size is summarised by the standard deviation.
A scrolling strip chart: the newest sample is at the edge, older samples move away, as on a seismograph.
The dashed line joining a photograph to its place on a chart, so that picture and number can be compared.

remember: Each plotted point is one frame reduced to one number: a segmentation, a scale and a definition.
Multiply pixels by the pixel scale to get millimetres, and quote the scale with its uncertainty.
Fluctuation is the signal minus its mean; its amplitude is the standard deviation, and its dimensionless size is the coefficient of variation.
The time between samples is 1/frame rate, so the fastest oscillation visible is half the frame rate.
Axis ranges that differ between panels or runs forbid comparing heights by eye.

understand.title: Why sample frames next to the traces
understand.text: A trace can look plausible and still be wrong. Putting six real photographs next to the numbers extracted from them lets a reader audit the segmentation without trusting the code.

understand.title: Why height and width are drawn separately
understand.text: They answer different questions. Height shows stretching and puffing; width shows bulging. Plotting them on the same axis would hide the smaller signal, so they get their own panels sharing one time axis.

understand.title: Why a scrolling strip
understand.text: The seismograph view puts the measured numbers on the screen at the same moment as the flame, so a viewer can see a taller flame and the trace move together in real time.

understand.title: The seismograph pair
understand.text: The onset frame (163 to 183 s) shows a flame of about 55 to 88 mm with a gentle wiggle; the developed frame (383 to 403 s) shows a taller flame with sharper spikes. The two use different axis ranges.

steps.title: From pixels to millimetres
steps.note: One reference length of known size gives the scale. Every later number in mm is the pixel count times this scale.

steps.title: Time stamp of a frame
steps.note: With 24 frames per second consecutive samples are one twenty-fourth of a second apart. The frame rate sets the finest time detail on the chart.

steps.title: Remove the mean
steps.note: The fluctuation is what is left once the average height is subtracted. Averages are taken over a window in which the flame is statistically steady.

steps.title: Size of the fluctuation
steps.note: The standard deviation is in mm; the coefficient of variation is dimensionless, so that tall and short flames or different runs can be compared.

steps.title: Uncertainty of one reading
steps.note: The scale error is multiplied by the height in pixels, so tall flames carry a larger scale error. The edge-position error is one or a few pixels times the scale.

steps.title: What the window can show
steps.note: A window of length T cannot resolve frequencies closer than 1/T, and the frame rate cannot show anything above half the frame rate.

worked.title: Convert a pixel height to millimetres, with an illustrative scale
worked.problem: Suppose a reference object 10 mm long spans 140 px in the frame, and the segmentation reports a flame length of 1456 px (the value printed on one overlay in this group). What is the height, and how much does a 2 percent scale error change it?

solution.text: A 2 percent error in the scale is a 2 percent error in h.

worked.answer: About 104 mm with about 2 mm from the scale alone. The 10 mm and 140 px are illustrative, not measured values; the real scale is set in the calibration step of the project.

analyze.q: In figure 06 the width trace has a burst to about 20 mm near 445 s while the height trace shows no matching extreme. What kind of flame motion produces a width burst without a height change?
analyze.hint: Look at the frame sampled at 443 s.

analyze.q: Figures 13 and 19 use different width axes (up to about 20 mm and about 65 mm). What conclusions are safe to draw by comparing them, and which are not?
analyze.hint: Compare values read off the tick labels, not trace shapes.

analyze.q: A single frame in the height trace is 40 mm above its neighbours. Give two causes, one physical and one a measurement artefact, and a check for each.
analyze.hint: Frame-by-frame inspection of the overlay, and the time scale of real flame motion.

evaluate.q: Is it enough to show six photographs to validate a trace of several thousand frames? What additional audit would you add?
evaluate.hint: Random sampling, worst-case frames, and a comparison with hand-measured heights.

evaluate.q: Is it a problem that the seismograph strips for the two runs are not on the same axes?
evaluate.hint: Consider a viewer who wants to judge how much more the developed flame fluctuates.

create: Redraw figure 06 with a small strip under the height trace marking the frames whose segmentation was inspected by hand, and with the pixel scale printed.
Design a seismograph frame that shows a fixed-range, shared-axis strip so that two runs can be compared directly, and a ghost line for the run's own mean.

checks.q: What does one point on the height trace represent?
checks.answer: One frame of the video, after segmentation, reduced to a single number: the distance from the burner rim to the flame tip, in mm.

checks.q: A flame is 1200 px long and the scale is 0.07 mm per pixel. What is its height?
A trace shows one frame at twice the height of its neighbours. Does it show a real flame event?
checks.hint: How fast can the flame change height between two frames?
checks.answer: Probably not. A flame cannot double its height within one frame time of about 0.04 s; it is more likely a detached piece or a bad segmentation. Look at the overlay for that frame.

checks.q: Two seismograph strips look equally jagged. Can you say the two flames fluctuate equally?
checks.answer: No. The strips have different axis ranges, so equal jaggedness on the page is not equal amplitude. Compare the numbers on the axes, or the coefficient of variation.

checks.q: How would you let a reader audit the segmentation?
checks.answer: Show sampled frames with their detected contour next to the trace, joined by leader lines, include worst-case frames as well as typical ones, and state the pixel scale and edge-position tolerance.
